result:
The kettle clicks off at 6:14. There is no ceremony, no music, no intention beyond the mechanical fact that water has reached its limit and must stop being heated. I stand in the kitchen in my undershirt, watching the steam curl in a slow, shapeless column, thinking about how much of a life is made of moments no one would call significant.

The spoon scraping the bottom of the mug. The small brown clouds where hot water meets grounds. The particular way the first sip tastes like the end of sleep and the beginning of obligation, all at once. The window behind me is still dark, but the sky is no longer *dark*—just very, very grey, and this distinction is doing most of the work the coming sun will do by noon.

I think we are taught to look for peaks. Promotions, proposals, moments that make a good caption on a card. But a life is mostly the flat, warm middle. The Tuesday where nothing happens. The coffee that is slightly too hot, then too cold, then just right, and by the time it is just right, you have already finished it.

The window fogs where my breath reaches it. I leave the mark. I don't wipe it clean.

Outside, a car passes. Just a car. Just the sound of it, sliding past like a thought you almost had.

I set the mug down. The day has started. It didn't ask my permission.
